name: HD 209458 b
significanceText: Nicknamed "Osiris," this was the first exoplanet ever caught transiting its star, and the first to have its atmosphere directly detected — a discovery that opened the entire field of exoplanet atmospheric science.

name: Kepler-186 f
significanceText: The first Earth-sized world ever confirmed inside another star's habitable zone, proving that rocky, temperate planets aren't unique to our solar system.

name: Kepler-452 b
significanceText: Dubbed Earth's "older cousin," it's the first near-Earth-size planet found orbiting a true Sun-like star in the habitable zone, offering a glimpse of what Earth might resemble 1.5 billion years from now.

name: TRAPPIST-1 b
significanceText: The innermost of the seven TRAPPIST-1 worlds, sitting too close to its star for liquid water but a key JWST target for testing whether small, hot rocky planets can hold onto any atmosphere at all.

name: TRAPPIST-1 c
significanceText: A Venus-sized, likely Venus-like world whose JWST observations found no evidence of a thick atmosphere, making it an important data point for how close-in rocky planets fare around flare-prone red dwarfs.

name: TRAPPIST-1 d
significanceText: The lightest of the seven, sitting right at the inner edge of the habitable zone — small enough that its history and possible volatile content are still hotly debated.

name: TRAPPIST-1 e
significanceText: Widely considered the most Earth-like planet in the system — similar density, squarely in the habitable zone — and one of the top targets in the search for a rocky exoplanet atmosphere.

name: TRAPPIST-1 f
significanceText: A cooler habitable-zone world that could host a global ocean if it retains enough of an atmosphere to stay warm despite its dim, distant-feeling host star.

name: TRAPPIST-1 g
significanceText: The largest of the seven planets, likely volatile-rich, and part of the tight orbital resonance chain that let astronomers precisely pin down the whole system's architecture.

name: TRAPPIST-1 h
significanceText: The outermost and coldest of the seven, likely an ice world — its predicted orbit, confirmed only through the system's three-body resonances, was one of the cleanest wins for resonance-based planet-hunting.
